sources.title: AAIB Bulletin No: 6/2002, Airbus Industrie A300B4-605R, G-MONS, incident at London Gatwick, 1 February 2002 (Ref: EW/C2002/02/05)
sources.publisher: UK Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB), Department for Transport
sources.page: Page 1 (report text): 'The manufacturer's maximum computed and demonstrated crosswind for the aircraft is 32 kt.'

pressurised.note: AC chapter 2.1 p. 2A gives a 'Pressurized Fuselage Volume' of 860 m3 (30 370 ft3) for the A300B4-600R.

cruise_kts.calculation: Airbus gives the A300-600/A310 family's Optimum Mach Number as 0.79 for GE engines (Getting to grips with the cost index, section 7 p. 47); this variant has GE CF6-80C2 engines. Typical cruise altitude FL300 (below). ISA at 30,000 ft: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 30000 = 228.71 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(228.71/288.15) = 589.3 kt; TAS = 0.79 x 589.3 = 465.6 -> 465 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Airbus's own guide (tier 2) gives the Optimum Mach, replacing the Aircraft Commerce LRC figure of the research pass (same 0.79). The Mach is for the A300-600/A310 family on GE engines (the guide's A300-600 tables are PW4158). Same method as the A310 entry.

min_runway_ft.calculation: WV004 weights (TCDS 17.3 p. 50; AC 2.1 pp. 2A-2B): MTOW 171,700 kg, MLW 140,000 kg. Take-off weight midway = 155,850 kg = 343,590 lb = 343.6 x 1000 lb. AC 3.3 p. 2 (FAR take-off runway length, ISA, GE CF6-80C2, model A300-600), sea-level ('0') curve read at 300 dpi against the gridlines (weight verticals 340 and 360 x 1000 lb, runway-length horizontals 6 and 7 x 1000 ft): at 343.6 x 1000 lb the curve lies 0.25 of the way from the 6,000 ft line to the 7,000 ft line = about 6,250 ft (flaps 15 / slats 20 region). Landing at MLW 140,000 kg = 308,647 lb: AC 3.4 p. 1 (FAR landing field length, slats 30 / flaps 40, all ambient temperatures), sea-level curve (lowest; weight verticals 250/300/350 x 1000 lb, length horizontals 5 and 6 x 1000 ft) at 308.6 x 1000 lb: about 5,110 ft. Longer = take-off 6,250 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,300 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Chart read from a scanned raster page (accuracy about +/-40 ft). The AC names no normal-operation flap setting; the take-off chart's regions are 15/20 and 15/15 (flaps/slats) and the reading lies in the 15/20 region. The chart is the AC's A300-600 chart for GE CF6-80C2 engines, plotted to 360 x 1000 lb, which covers the midpoint weight.

ceiling_ft.note: Maximum authorized altitude 40 000 ft (12 200 m), TCDS EASA.A.172 Issue 08, Section 20 item 20.9, p. 63 of 68 (common to the -600 series; Note 6's 35,000 ft applies only to certain F4-600R weight variants).

max_xwind_kts.note: Stated by the AAIB for an A300B4-605R (CF6-80C2A5) as 'the manufacturer's maximum computed and demonstrated crosswind for the aircraft'; the demonstrations assumed a steady-state crosswind, and the operator adopted 32 kt as its A300 fleet limit. A government report quoting the manufacturer, not read from the AFM; the TCDS gives no crosswind limit.

cruise_alt_ft.note: Airbus's 'first optimum flight level' for the A300 at high take-off weights (MTOW - 10 t to MTOW), ISA+10: FL300 (section 6.2 table p. 30; FL280 at ISA+20). Same convention as the A310 entry. Below the 40,000 ft ceiling.

climb_fpm.note: Airliner class preset. The Airbus guide's Table 6 (climb to FL330) and Table 15 (descent from FL370) give the A300-600 only with PW4158 engines at 150 t / 120 t, not this variant's GE engines, so no accepted source gives the variant's own time.

climb_kts.note: Airliner class preset: 90% of the 465 kt cruise speed = 418.5 -> 420 kt.

descent_fpm.note: Airliner class preset; the guide's descent tables for the A300-600 are PW4158 only (see climb rate).

cruise_kts.calculation: Airbus's payload-range chart for the B4-203 (AC chapter 3 p. 8) gives the cruise as 'M = 0.78 CRUISE AT 33,000 FT / 35,000 FT'. At 33,000 ft (ISA): T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 33000 = 222.8 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(222.8/288.15) = 581.6 kt; TAS = 0.78 x 581.6 = 453.7 -> 455 kt.

Landing at MLW 136,000 kg = 299,828 lb: AC chapter 3 p. 35 (FAR landing field length, dry runway, no wind, flaps 25 / slats 25, all ambient temperatures), curve for airport altitude 0 (lowest) at 299.8 x 1000 lb: about 6,300 ft. Longer = take-off 6,413 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,500 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Charts read from the scanned pages (accuracy about +/-40 ft); take-off governs, landing is close (6,300). The landing chart is for flaps 25/slats 25 (the TCDS limits MLW 136,000 kg to slats 16/flaps 15 and 134,000 kg to slats 25/flaps 25); at 134,000 kg landing is shorter still.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Take-off weight midway between MLW 140,000 kg and MTOW 170,500 kg (AC 2.1 p. 2, WV000) = 155,250 kg = 342,267 lb = 342.3 x 1000 lb. Landing at MLW 140,000 kg = 308,646 lb: AC 3.4 p. 1 (FAR landing field length, slats 30 / flaps 40, all ambient temperatures), sea-level curve (the lowest, rightmost one; weight lines 80-400 x 1000 lb, length lines 3-8 x 1000 ft) at 308.6 x 1000 lb: about 4,910 ft. pressurised.note: AC 2.1.1 p. 3 gives the A310's 'Pressurized Fuselage Volume' (680 m3, A/C non equipped).

cruise_kts.calculation: Airbus gives the Optimum Mach Number of the A310-304 as 0.79 (Getting to grips with the cost index, Figure 35 p. 50, at the typical cruise conditions FL350; and §7 p. 47, 'on the A300-600/A310 family the Optimum Mach Number is set at 0.79 (GE)'); the A310-304 has GE CF6-80C2A2 engines (TCDS 13.2). ISA at 35,000 ft: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81 / 288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.79 x 576.4 = 455.4 -> 455 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Airbus's 'Optimum Mach' (the Mach of greatest specific range at the given weight and level) is the only cruise Mach published for the -304; the same figure's LRC Mach is 0.803, and Figure 26 p. 41 shows ECON Mach about 0.80 at cost index 60.

min_runway_ft.calculation: WV05 weights (TCDS 13.3 p. 38; AC 2.1.1 p. 3): MTOW 157,000 kg = 346,125 lb, MLW 124,000 kg = 273,372 lb. Takeoff weight midway = 309,748 lb. AC 3.3.1 p. 4 (ISA, GE CF6-80C2, Model 300), sea-level (0) curve, read from the scan against its gridlines (weight gridlines every 10 klb, runway gridlines every 500 ft; the 0 curve at 309.75 klb crosses 14,000 - (780.6 - 232.4) / 69.64 x 1,000 ft in render coordinates): about 6,130 ft of runway. Landing at MLW 273,372 lb: AC 3.4.1 p. 1 (flaps 40, slats 30; the chart gives the field length, = actual distance / 0.6), sea-level (0) curve: about 5,100 ft. Longer = takeoff 6,130 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,200 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Readings from the scanned charts by pixel measurement against the gridlines (about +/-100 ft; the checker reads 6,130 ft, the researcher 6,160 ft, both round to 6,200). The takeoff chart is the only GE CF6-80C2 Model 300 ISA chart; its weight axis runs 200-360 klb. The AC's heaviest weight variants (WV008/WV013, MTOW 164,000 kg) are certified for the A310-308/-325, not the -304, so WV05 is used.

ceiling_ft.note: Maximum authorized altitude for 'A310 all series – all models' (section 14.9). Pressure altitude not stated, 41,100 ft (12,530 m).

cruise_alt_ft.note: Airbus's Figure 35 (p. 50, 'A310 ECON Mach', specific example for the A310-304) marks 'TYPICAL CRUISE CONDITIONS' at FL350 beside the Optimum Mach of 0.79. (The earlier choice, FL330, was the guide's first optimum flight level at high takeoff weight, §6.2 p. 30, ISA+10; FL310 at ISA+20.)

climb_fpm.calculation: Getting to grips with the cost index, Table 6 p. 21 (A310, CF6-80, 140,000 kg, climb to FL330, ISA, no wind, 250 kt up to FL100), cost index 60: climb-only segment time 17.7 min. 33,000 / 17.7 = 1,864 → 1,850 fpm.
climb_fpm.note: Cost index 60 is the tabulated value nearest the medium time / medium fuel cost cell of Table 1 p. 10 (65 kg/min). Other rows: CI 0 17.4 min (→ 1,900 fpm), CI 200 18.2 min (→ 1,800 fpm). The published weight is 140,000 kg, not the variant's MTOW; taken as published.

climb_kts.calculation: Table 6 p. 21 (A310, CF6-80, 140,000 kg, climb to FL330, ISA, no wind), cost index 60: 121 nm in 17.7 min. 121 / (17.7 / 60) = 410.2 → 410 kt.
climb_kts.note: Distance and time to FL330 taken as published. CI 0: 114 nm / 17.4 min → 395 kt; CI 200: 127 nm / 18.2 min → 420 kt.

descent_fpm.calculation: Table 15 p. 53 (A310, CF6-80, 110,000 kg, descent from FL370, ISA, no wind, 250 kt below FL100), cost index 60: descent-only segment time 17 min. 37,000 / 17 = 2,176 → 2,200 fpm.
descent_fpm.note: The published descent is from FL370, not from the FL330 cruise altitude, and its end point is not stated; taken as published, not corrected (33,000 / 17 would give 1,950 fpm). CI 0: 21.4 min (→ 1,750 fpm); CI 100: 15.3 min (→ 2,400 fpm).

pressurised.note: AC 2-1-1 p. 2 gives the A340-600 a 'Pressurized Fuselage Volume' (1 305 m3).

cruise_kts.calculation: Manufacturer's cruise conditions printed on its payload/range chart: 'CRUISE CONDITIONS ISA 39000 ft M = 0.82' (AC 3-2-1 p. 2, FIGURE-3-2-1-991-018). At 39,000 ft (above 36,089 ft) T = 216.65 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(216.65/288.15) = 573.6 kt; TAS = 0.82 x 573.6 = 470.3 -> 470 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Airbus's own cruise conditions for the type (M0.82 at 39,000 ft, ISA), used as the typical cruise Mach and altitude; the AC gives no separate economy or maximum cruise figure.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Takeoff weight midway between MLW 265,000 kg and MTOW 380,000 kg (AC 2-1-1 p. 1, WV101; TCDS item 12 gives the same A340-6xx weights) = 322,500 kg. AC 3-3-1 p. 2 (take-off weight limitation, ISA, RB211 Trent 556, A340-600), 0 ft airport-pressure-altitude curve, read from the chart's vector curve against its gridlines (weight axis 180 to 440 x 1000 kg, runway length 1.5 to 5 x 1000 m) at 322.5 t: about 2,419 m = 7,938 ft (0 ft curve, Bezier segment, gridline-calibrated). Landing at MLW 265,000 kg: AC 3-4-1 p. 2 (landing field length, ISA, RB211 Trent 556), 0 ft elevation curve (weight 180 to 300 x 1000 kg, length 3.5 to 1.5 x 1000 m): about 2,211 m = 7,253 ft. Longer = takeoff 7,938 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 8,000 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: The charts give no flap setting. The Trent 553 charts (3-3-1 p. 3, 3-4-1 p. 3) are for the A340-500. The AC says the curves are for information only.

ceiling_ft.note: Certified maximum operating altitude, 41,450 ft (12,634 m) (item 10.1, Section 3 A340-600, p. 50 of 75).

max_xwind_kts.note: Certified wind-speed limitation of the aeroplane (TCDS item 11 'Wind Speed Limitations', gust included, no runway condition stated), not the demonstrated crosswind: the TCDS itself says 'Refer to approved Aeroplane Flight Manual for maximum demonstrated crosswind', and no accepted source quotes that figure for this type. Used as the manufacturer-certified crosswind guidance, the highest-ranked source that gives a numeric crosswind; being gust-inclusive and a limit it is on the conservative side of a demonstrated steady value. The A330 TCDS (EASA.A.004) carries no numeric crosswind limit, so the A330 entries stay blank. TCDS Section 3 (A340-600), item 11, p. 50 of 75: takeoff 35 kt, landing 37 kt (gust included); the lower, 35 kt. AAIB Bulletin 7/2007 (G-VSHY): 'The operator's aircraft manual for the A340-600 states that the maximum demonstrated crosswind for a manual landing, including gusts, is 37 kt', equal to the TCDS landing limit, a landing value only, quoted from an operator's manual; no demonstrated takeoff value is available, so the TCDS takeoff limit of 35 kt is the lower figure.

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude of Airbus's printed cruise conditions (ISA 39000 ft, M = 0.82, AC 3-2-1 p. 2, FIGURE-3-2-1-991-018); below the 41,450 ft ceiling.

climb_fpm.note: Airliner class preset; neither the AC nor the TCDS gives a time to climb.

climb_kts.note: Airliner class preset: 90% of the 470 kt cruise speed = 423 -> 425 kt.

descent_fpm.note: Airliner class preset; neither the AC nor the TCDS gives a descent time or rate.

pressurised.note: AC 2-1-0 p. 3 gives the A350-900's 'Unequipped Pressurized Volume' (1313 m3).

cruise_kts.calculation: Airbus publishes a cruise Mach of 0.85 for the A350-900 (technical specifications, Performance). It gives no altitude, so the table's typical cruise altitude (the Airliner preset's 35,000 ft) is used. ISA at 35,000 ft: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81/288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.85 x 576.4 = 489.9 -> 490 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Published as 'Cruise Mach' 0.85 without a stated altitude or the words 'typical' or 'economy'. Confirmed on the page.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Variant WV020: MLW 207,000 kg (AC 2-1-0 p. 3; TCDS item 1.7), MTOW 283,000 kg (TCDS item 1.7; Airbus specification page 283.00 t). The AC's WV020 MTOW cell reads 283900 kg, equal to its Maximum Taxi/Ramp Weight cell and to the ramp weight its pavement chapter gives for WV020, so it is read as the ramp weight and the certified MTOW is used. Takeoff weight midway = (207,000 + 283,000) / 2 = 245,000 kg. AC 3-3-0 p. 2 (A350-900, ISA, dry runway), 0 ft pressure-altitude curve, read from the chart's vector geometry against its gridlines (weight axis 150-290 t, runway axis 1,500-5,500 m) at 245 t: about 2,076 m = 6,810 ft. Landing at MLW 207,000 kg, AC 3-4-0 p. 2 (0 ft curve, valid for all temperatures; the curve ends at 205 t, extended 2 t along its last slope): about 1,990 m = 6,530 ft. Longer = takeoff 6,810 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,900 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Read accuracy about 1% (about 50 ft). Chart is drawn for MTOW 280 t; 245 t lies inside the plotted range. WV023 (280,000/205,000 kg) would give about 6,664 ft -> 6,700 ft.

ceiling_ft.note: Certified maximum operating altitude, 43,100 ft (TCDS item 2.7, p. 14, all A350-900 series).

cruise_alt_ft.note: Airliner class preset; Airbus's A350 pages give no typical cruise altitude.

climb_kts.note: Airliner class preset: 90% of the 490 kt cruise speed = 441.0 -> 440 kt.

The printed feet scale (5,000-18,000 ft) is not an exact conversion of the metre scale and reads about 6,700 ft (on the rounding line, 6,800 ft if it rounded up); the metre axis is used. entries.name: Commander 114
entries.variant: Gulfstream/Rockwell Commander 114 (S/N 14150 and subsequent: normally aspirated Lycoming IO-540-T4B5D, 260 hp, Hartzell two-blade constant speed propeller; maximum gross weight 3,140 lb). SimBrief's 'Commander 114' covers the 114, 114A and 114B (type certificate A12SO); the 114's own handbook is the highest-tier source found, the 114B having only AOPA figures

sources.title: Gulfstream Commander 114 Pilot's Operating Handbook, P/N M114001-1 (issued 21 February 1976, Revision 11, 16 July 1986; 219-page scan, 'Commander Owners Group 2013' watermark)
sources.publisher: Gulfstream Aerospace Corporation (Rockwell Commander 114 handbook; scan hosted by the Commander Owners Group)
sources.page: p. 1-7 Demonstrated Crosswind Velocity 19 kts (PDF p. 13); Fig. 5-11 normal total takeoff distance, p. 5-27 (PDF 82); Fig. 5-36 short field total landing distance, p. 5-71 (PDF 126); Fig. 5-27 cruise true airspeed S/N 14150 & subs, p. 5-53 (PDF 108); Fig. 5-15 rate of climb S/N 14150 & subs, p. 5-35 (PDF 90); Fig. 5-17 time, distance and fuel in climb, p. 5-39 (PDF 94); Fig. 5-34 descent at 1,000 ft/min, p. 5-66/5-67 (PDF 121-122); Section VII Heating and Ventilation System, p. 7-24

pressurised.note: The handbook describes only a heating and ventilation system (Section VII, p. 7-24) and an optional oxygen system; it has no pressurisation system, controller or differential limit. No accepted source says 'unpressurised' in words (FAA TCDS A12SO could not be opened); this rests on the manual's silence about a system it would have to describe, as for the Cessna 172R entry.

cruise_kts.calculation: POH Fig. 5-27 (S/N 14150 & subs, 3,140 lb, best economy, ISA), 2500 rpm panel: the 75% MCP line is attainable up to where it meets the full-throttle line (about 7,300 ft ISA), where it is fastest; read there at 147.8 kt TAS (scale 100 kt and 140 kt ticks, 9.4 px/kt at 400 dpi). The 2400 rpm panel gives about 146 kt. 147.8 -> 150 kt (nearest 5).
cruise_kts.note: 75% power, best economy, at the altitude where that power is fastest (the top of the 75% MCP line), the meanings table's POH cruise; read from a scan to about +/-1 kt, so close to the 147.5 kt rounding edge. The 153 kt first read was the full-throttle curve's peak (about 4,700 ft), not 75% power. The maker's headline figure is not in the handbook.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Fig. 5-11 (normal takeoff, 10 deg flaps, 3,140 lb, dry level paved): ISA line meets the sea-level curve at about 14.7 C and 2,175 ft to the 50 ft height (axis ticks 2,000/3,000 ft 188 px apart at 400 dpi). Fig. 5-36 (landing from 50 ft, 3,140 lb): sea level at ISA about 1,200 ft. Longer = takeoff 2,175 -> 2,200 ft (up to next 100).
min_runway_ft.note: Read from the charts' curves at maximum gross weight, sea level, standard day, zero wind; over a 50 ft obstacle. AOPA's 114B figure (2,000 ft takeoff over 50 ft) is another variant.

ceiling_ft.calculation: Fig. 5-15 (rate of climb, S/N 14150 & subs, 3,140 lb): the ISA line crosses the 14,000 ft curve at about 175 fpm and the 16,000 ft curve at about 50 fpm; 100 fpm lies at 14,000 + 2,000 x (175-100)/(175-50) = 15,200 ft.
ceiling_ft.note: Service ceiling (rate of climb 100 fpm, ISA, maximum gross weight) read from the handbook's climb chart; no certified maximum operating altitude is given. Disagreement: AOPA Pilot July 1992 prints 16,800 ft for the 114B, and a brochure cited by Wikipedia gives 14,200 ft; both are another variant or not accepted, so the handbook's chart for this variant is used.

max_xwind_kts.note: POH p. 1-7: 'The demonstrated crosswind velocity (19kts) ... The value shown is not considered to be limiting.' Also the note in the balked landing procedure: 'Maximum demonstrated crosswind is 19 knots.'

cruise_alt_ft.calculation: The altitude the cruise speed is read at: POH Fig. 5-27, the 75% power line is fastest where it meets the full-throttle line, at about 7,300 ft ISA -> 7,500 ft (nearest 500 ft).
cruise_alt_ft.note: Taken with the cruise speed, as the meanings table asks (the altitude where the cruise is quoted).

climb_fpm.calculation: Fig. 5-17 (time, distance and fuel in climb, S/N 14150 & subs, 3,140 lb, ISA): the ISA line crosses the 6,000 ft and 7,000 ft altitude lines at 862 and 785 px (300 dpi), so 6,500 ft is at 824 px; the climb curve there meets the time scale at 7.7 min from sea level (28.1 px/min). 6500 / 7.7 = 844 -> 850 fpm (nearest 50).
climb_fpm.note: Average from sea level to the preset cruise altitude of 6,500 ft, scheduled climb speeds, full throttle, standard day; time read from a scan to about +/-0.2 min (820-870 fpm).

climb_kts.calculation: Fig. 5-17 has a distance scale: the same curve point at 6,500 ft ISA meets the distance scale (ticks 10 nm at 1386 px, 20 nm at 1560 px) at 12.3 nm in 7.7 min: 12.3 / 7.7 x 60 = 95.8 kt (published distance / time, brief rule 13) -> 95 kt (nearest 5).
climb_kts.note: Average true airspeed over the climb's time from the published distance and time to climb; read from a scan to about +/-3 kt, rounding stays 95 over 92.5-97.5 kt.

descent_fpm.note: POH p. 5-66: the descent time, distance and fuel chart (Fig. 5-34) is presented for a 1000 FT/MIN rate of descent; the descent technique maintains 1,000 ft/min.

sources.page: Table, row 'Typical Cruise Speed (at 35,000 feet)', 737-700

cruise_kts.calculation: Boeing's 737-700 technical characteristics give the Next Generation 737-700 a typical cruise speed of Mach 0.785 at 35,000 ft. ISA at 35,000 ft: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81 / 288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.785 x 576.4 = 452.5 -> 450 kt.
cruise_kts.note: base type's figure (B737): the MAX 7 is a re-engined 737NG-family airplane and no accepted source gives its own cruise Mach. The maximum operating Mach was not independently confirmed from an accepted source.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Takeoff weight midway between MLW 145,600 lb and MTOW 177,000 lb (ACAP Sec. 2.1.1 p. 2-2) = 161,300 lb. ACAP Sec. 3.3.5 p. 3-13 (737-7 LEAP-1B28B2C, standard day, dry runway; axes 80-190 thousand lb and 3-15 thousand ft, gridlines every 5 thousand lb and 1,000 ft), sea-level curve (the lowest) at 161,300 lb: about 5,560 ft. Landing at MLW 145,600 lb, ACAP Sec. 3.4.2 p. 3-43 (flaps 30), dry sea-level curve (lowest dashed) at the maximum landing weight: about 5,200 ft. Longer = takeoff 5,560 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 5,600 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: The ACAP's takeoff and landing charts are raster images; each curve was read by pixel measurement against the drawn gridlines (axes calibrated on the chart frame and gridlines, sub-pixel curve centroid), good to about +/-30 ft. The 737-7's takeoff chart for the LEAP-1B25 (Sec. 3.3.1) was not used: the 177,000 lb MTOW is on the 1B28B2C chart.

cruise_alt_ft.note: Airliner class preset (35,000 ft) lowered to 12,000 ft because the entry's pressurisation is unknown (blank): no accepted source states the 737-7's pressurisation or maximum operating altitude (EASA TCDS Issue 29 does not list the 737-7; the FAA's data sheet could not be opened). Revisit if a source is found.

climb_kts.note: Airliner class preset: 90% of the 450 kt cruise speed = 405.0 -> 405 kt.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights (ACAP p. 9, -320C columns): MTOW 333,600 lb, MLW 247,000 lb; midpoint = (247,000 + 333,600) / 2 = 290,300 lb. Takeoff: ACAP p. 40 (C.A.R., JT3D-7, improved cowl doors, 14 degree flaps, upper chart 'STANDARD DAY'), sea-level curve at 290,300 lb. Read on a 300 dpi render: gridlines 280 klb x=1544.5 and 300 klb x=1780.5 (11.8 px/klb) put 290,300 lb at x=1666; 6 kft line y=846.6 and 8 kft line y=605.1 (120.75 px/kft); sea-level curve centre y=661.7; 6 + (846.6 - 661.7) / 120.75 = 7.531 kft = 7,531 ft. Landing at MLW 247,000 lb, ACAP p. 45, dry sea-level line: about 6.26 kft. Longer = takeoff 7,531 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 7,600 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: C.A.R. field lengths (the 707's certification basis), as the chart gives them. The chart's -320C maximum-takeoff-weight line is at about 335,000 lb (the wet-thrust weight): taking 335,000 lb for the maximum gives a midpoint of 291,000 lb and about 7,580 ft, still 7,600 ft. 14 degree flaps is the only setting plotted for this engine. Reading good to about +/-40 ft.

cruise_alt_ft.note: Airliner class preset 35,000 ft; no ceiling is published for the 707-320C by an accepted source (the 4A26 data sheet gives none), so the preset is not lowered; the type is pressurised (see pressurised).

cruise_kts.note: Boeing's own 504 mph (438 kt) on the same row does not equal M0.77 at 34,200 ft in the standard atmosphere; the Mach and altitude are used.

Takeoff: Fig. 3.3.5 (printed p. 27, dry, standard day, BR715 at 21,000 lb thrust), sea-level curve at 115,500 lb, read on an 8x render against the frame and gridlines (grid check: the 5 kft gridline reads 5.003 kft, the 115 klb gridline 114.98 klb): 4.993 kft read, 4.990 after the grid correction = 4,990 ft. Landing at MLW 110,000 lb: Fig. 3.4.1 (printed p. 31, flaps 40, dry, sea level, standard day), dry sea-level curve read 4.968 kft at 109.5 klb and 4.918 at 108 klb, so about 4.985 kft at 110 klb = 4,985 ft. Longer = takeoff 4,990 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 5,000 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Takeoff and landing are within 10 ft of each other, and the takeoff reading sits right on the 5,000 ft rounding line (chart readings are good to about +/-20 ft); if the true figure is above 5,000 ft the rule gives 5,100. The ACAP has one landing chart (flaps 40).

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights (ACAP p. 9, heaviest optional column): maximum flight weight 169,000 lb (the -100 table gives no separate maximum takeoff weight), MLW 142,500 lb; midpoint = (142,500 + 169,000) / 2 = 155,750 lb. Landing at MLW 142,500 lb, ACAP p. 51, 30 degree flaps, dry sea-level line: about 5.3 kft. Longer = takeoff 6,300 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: C.A.R. field lengths as the chart gives them (flap setting by the chart's envelope at that weight). Good to about +/-50 ft. The -100 table lists no maximum takeoff weight, so the maximum flight weight stands in for it.

ceiling_ft.note: Certified maximum operating altitude. Boeing's brochure gives a lower 'ceiling' of 36,100 ft (a service ceiling), not used.

cruise_alt_ft.note: Airliner preset 35,000 ft (within the 42,000 ft ceiling; the type is pressurised); no accepted source gives a typical cruise altitude for the 727-100 (the ACAP's payload/range charts, p. 30, use long-range cruise at 30,000 and 35,000 ft).

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights (ACAP p. 11, Advanced options column): MTOW 209,500 lb, MLW 161,000 lb; midpoint = (161,000 + 209,500) / 2 = 185,250 lb. Takeoff: ACAP p. 45, JT8D-15, standard day, sea-level curve, read from a 300 dpi render against the printed gridlines near the curve (weight gridlines 180 klb at x=1603 px and 190 klb at x=1846 px, 24.3 px per klb, so 185,250 lb is at x=1731 px; length gridlines 8 kft at y=1631.5 px and 7 kft at y=1875 px, 243.5 px per kft; the curve's centre line at x=1731 px is at y=1742-1746 px): 7 + (1875 - 1744) / 243.5 = 7.54 kft = about 7,540 ft. Landing at MLW 161,000 lb, ACAP p. 53, 30 degree flaps (the 40 degree chart stops at 158,000 lb), dry sea-level line: about 4.95 kft. Longer = takeoff 7,540 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 7,600 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: C.A.R. field lengths as the chart gives them. The midpoint falls on the steep step of the sea-level curve where the flap setting changes (the step spans 184.9 klb / 7.44 kft to 186.2 klb / 7.87 kft), so the reading is good to about +/-50 ft; read in a straight line along the plotted step. The JT8D-17 chart (p. 47) is a near-identical curve.

The chart's sea-level curve is the optimum-flap line (flaps 15 changing to flaps 5); landing flaps 40 is the shortest of the three landing charts. Reading good to about +/-30 ft.

pressurised.calculation: The UK AAIB's bulletin on a 737-436 (G-DOCE, p. 2) describes the 737-400's cabin pressure control system regulating air outflow from 'the pressurised section of the fuselage'. The FAA TCDS also certifies the type to 37,000 ft (p. 17), and Boeing's 737 Family Background gives 37,000 ft as the 737-300/-400/-500's maximum altitude. cruise_kts.calculation: Boeing's technical characteristics for the 737-400 give a typical cruise speed of Mach 0.745 at 35,000 ft (495 mph). ISA at 35,000 ft: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81 / 288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.745 x 576.4 = 429.4 -> 430 kt.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights for the CFM56-3B-2 (22,000 lb) column, ACAP §2.1.7: MTOW 150,000 lb, MLW 124,000 lb; midpoint = 137,000 lb. Takeoff, ACAP §3.3.15 (F.A.R. standard day, CFM56-3B-2 at 22,000 lb SLST, zero wind, no bleed): the sea-level curve read by pixel measurement against the drawn axes and gridlines (calibrated on the 105 and 135 klb gridlines and the 7 and 6 kft gridlines) gives 6,667 ft at 136,000 lb, 6,957 ft at 137,000 lb, 7,234 ft at 138,000 lb. Landing, ACAP §3.4.14 (flaps 30), dry sea-level curve at the chart's maximum landing weight 124,000 lb: about 5,370 ft (5,344 ft read at 123,500 lb, extended along the curve's slope). Longer = takeoff 6,957 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 7,000 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Readings are good to about +/-30 ft; the takeoff reading would have to exceed 7,000 ft by more than 43 ft to change the rounded figure. The takeoff chart is a single curve family per elevation (flaps 5 / flaps 15 switch is built into each curve), so no flap choice applied. Landing never governs: the chart gives three flap settings (40, 30, 15) with no normal one named; the longest, flaps 15, reads about 6,100 ft at MLW, still below the takeoff figure.

entries.name: Beechcraft C24R

sources.title: Beechcraft Sierra C24R Pilot's Operating Handbook and FAA Approved Airplane Flight Manual, P/N 169-590025-15B, reissued November 1980, revised July 1994 (complete scan)
sources.publisher: Raytheon Aircraft Company (Beech Aircraft Corporation); scan hosted by befa.org
sources.page: Section IV p. 4-3 (maximum demonstrated crosswind component); Section V p. 5-18 (take-off distance, hard surface), p. 5-21 (time, fuel and distance to climb), p. 5-27 (cruise speeds), p. 5-33 (landing distance, hard surface); Section I p. 1-10 (weights); Section VII p. 7-33 (ventilation)

sources.page: Specifications: Performance, 'Service ceiling (ft.): 14,342'

pressurised.note: Section VII (p. 7-33) describes cabin ventilation by fresh-air inlets and eyeball outlets only, and Section X's safety text speaks of 'unpressurized airplanes' at altitude; no pressurisation system or cabin differential appears anywhere in the handbook. Rests on the handbook's silence.

cruise_kts.calculation: Cruise Speeds chart, p. 5-27 (average weight 2,600 lb, standard day): the 75% lines (2700 rpm and 2500 rpm) meet the full-throttle curve for 2700 rpm at 10,000 ft, the highest altitude at which 75% power is available, where TAS reads 136.9 kt. 136.9 -> 135 kt (nearest 5 kt). At 8,000 ft the 2500 rpm line reads 134 kt; at sea level 125 kt.
cruise_kts.note: No headline cruise figure in the handbook; chart read from the page image, +-1 kt.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Take-Off Distance - Hard Surface, p. 5-18 (flaps 15 deg, paved level dry; lift-off 66 kt, 50 ft at 71 kt), re-read by pixel measurement: sea level curve at 15 C (ISA), 2,750 lb (on the weight reference line, so no weight correction), no wind: ground roll about 1,120 ft, total over a 50 ft obstacle about 1,620-1,630 ft. Landing Distance - Hard Surface, p. 5-33 (flaps down, maximum braking, 70 kt approach at 2,750 lb): sea level, 15 C, 2,750 lb, no wind: ground roll about 830 ft, total over 50 ft about 1,430-1,470 ft. The longer is the takeoff: about 1,630 -> 1,700 ft (next 100 ft).
min_runway_ft.note: Both read from the nomograms by following the example's procedure; reading uncertainty about +-50 ft, which leaves the takeoff total below 1,700 ft. Maximum landing weight equals maximum takeoff weight (2,750 lb, Section I p. 1-10).

ceiling_ft.note: Plane & Pilot's specifications table for the 1977 C24R Sierra 200 (fourth tier: neither the handbook nor a data sheet gives a service ceiling; the page quotes no issue or page, only its web address). 14,342 ft is as printed.

max_xwind_kts.note: 'Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Component 17 KTS / 20 MPH' (Section IV p. 4-3, Speeds for Safe Operation); a demonstrated value, not a limitation.

cruise_alt_ft.calculation: The altitude of the 75% cruise speed above (p. 5-27): 10,000 ft, where 75% power at 2700 rpm is fastest and still available at full throttle. Below the 12,000 ft unpressurised cap and the 14,342 ft ceiling.

climb_fpm.calculation: Time, Fuel and Distance to Climb, p. 5-21 (96 kt climb speed, 2700 rpm, full throttle, flaps and gear up, from sea level): 10,000 ft at ISA (-5 C) is the 11.9 GPH altitude line at -5 C; carried across to the 2,750 lb curve it reads 17.1 min. 10000 / 17.1 = 585 -> 600 fpm.
climb_fpm.note: Chart read by pixel measurement against the axes; the chart's own example reads 22.3 min where it prints 23, so about +-0.6 min. Fuel for start and takeoff is separate.

climb_kts.calculation: Same chart, p. 5-21: the vertical through 17.1 min meets the nonlinear distance-to-climb scale at about 29.6 NM. 29.6 NM / (17.1/60 h) = 104 kt -> 105 kt (nearest 5 kt).
climb_kts.note: Zero-wind air distance. The chart's climb speed is a constant 96 KIAS.

descent_fpm.note: No published descent rate or time to descend in the handbook; Piston single class preset.

ceiling_ft.note: No certified maximum operating altitude for the normally aspirated A36 in TCDS 3A15, so the manufacturer's published service ceiling (100 fpm) is used: 18,500 ft at 3,650 lb.

The same 17 kt is published for the B36TC (AOPA Pilot, Jan 2000).

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude at which the normal-cruise-power speed above is quoted (fastest of 6,000 / 8,000 / 10,000 ft). Unpressurised: oxygen is required above 12,500 ft only; 8,000 ft is within the 12,000 ft limit for unpressurised types.

climb_fpm.calculation: POH p. 5-25, Time, Fuel, and Distance to Cruise Climb (full throttle, 2500 rpm, 110 kt): cruise pressure altitude 8,000 ft, ISA (OAT -1 C), from sea level, initial climb weight 3650 lb (the heaviest curve): time read from the 3650 curve at the 8,000 ft line = about 10.5 min (read 10-11 min). 8000 / 10.5 = 762 -> 750 fpm (the rounding is the same for 10.1-11.1 min).
climb_fpm.note: Time to climb to the table's cruise altitude (8,000 ft) at max gross weight, full throttle; chart read by eye.

climb_kts.calculation: POH p. 5-25: the distance scale (0-80 nm) and the time scale (0-40 min) span the same width, so distance/time = 2.0 nm/min = 120 kt at any time read (the chart's own example: 23.5 nm / 11.5 min = 2.04 nm/min). Consistent with 110 KIAS: TAS about 110 at sea level to about 124 at 8,000 ft ISA.
climb_kts.note: Average speed over the climb: distance to climb divided by time to climb.

sources.page: Article text: 'the design cruise speed of Mach 0.785'; 'The highest altitude so far has been 39,800 ft. (12,100 m) ... the maximum intended for operation'; the web edition carries no page numbers

pressurised.calculation: COMAC's own Crash Fire Rescue Chart describes 'Pressurization Preventing Door' mechanisms and a CABIN PRESSURE indicator light to check before opening a door, and the ICAO working paper gives a maximum operating altitude of 39,800 ft: a pressurised cabin.
pressurised.note: No accepted source found that says 'pressurised' in so many words (CAAC TCDS not found in English; EASA validation not complete).

cruise_kts.note: Fourth tier (Aviation Week, 11 Feb 2020, a flight-test report quoting COMAC's 'design cruise speed of Mach 0.785'); no source of the first three tiers gives a cruise Mach (the ACAP, the ICAO paper and COMAC's product page do not). The same article reports flight tests reaching M0.82; its 39,800 ft agrees with the ICAO paper's ceiling. The article names no altitude, so 35,000 ft (the preset altitude) is used.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights (ACAP 02-01 Table 1, ER column): MTOW 78,900 kg, MLW 67,800 kg; midpoint = (67,800 + 78,900) / 2 = 73,350 kg. Takeoff, sea level, ISA, Table 6 Config 3 (the shortest of the three takeoff configurations, since the ACAP names no normal one): 72,000 kg 1660 m, 74,300 kg 1760 m; at 73,350 kg = 1660 + (1350 / 2300) x 100 = 1718.7 m = 5,639 ft (Config 1+F, the longest, gives 1804 + (1350 / 2300) x 100 = 1862.7 m = 6,111 ft). Landing at MLW 67,800 kg, dry, flaps FULL (the shorter of the two landing flap settings): 1832 + ((67,800 - 65,000) / 5,000) x (1911 - 1832) = 1876.2 m = 6,155.5 ft. Longer = landing 6,155.5 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,200 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: The ACAP's required landing distance on a dry runway is the demonstrated distance divided by 0.6. With flaps 3 the landing figure is 1899 m = 6,230 ft (6,300 ft). The ACAP names no normal landing flap setting, so the shorter (FULL) is used. The standard-range version has the same landing figures. The ACAP's copyright statement forbids quotation without COMAC's written authorisation; figures are used as data. The ICAO working paper (WP/26 Table 1) lists takeoff field length at MTOW, SL, ISA 2,052 m (STD) / 2,125 m (ER), which match the ACAP's Config 1+F tables at MTOW (2,125 m ER), but its landing field length line (2,043 m / 2,133 m) does not match the ACAP's landing tables at the MLW (1,876 m dry, FULL; 1,900 m flaps 3); the ACAP, the higher-ranked source, wins. With the ICAO landing figure the runway would be about 6,800 ft.

ceiling_ft.note: ICAO WP/26 Table 1: 'Max Operating Altitude 12131 m (39800 ft)', both versions. The ACAP's own APU data module (02-12) also states 12131 m (39,800 ft) but there as the APU's in-flight limit. Presented by China; the CAAC type certificate data sheet was not found in English.

sources.page: Section 1.6.2 (Factual Information, printed p. 12): pneumatic system 'also supplied air to the cabin pressurization system, which was digitally controlled to maintain a maximum cabin altitude of 8,000 feet'

pressurised.note: NTSB's report on a CL-600-2B19 describes its digitally controlled cabin pressurization system (maximum cabin altitude 8,000 ft; cabin altitude warning at 10,000 ft).

cruise_kts.calculation: Normal cruise Mach 0.74 (Aircraft Commerce issue 66, CRJ-100/CRJ-200; no Bombardier or authority document found giving the type's cruise Mach). At 37,000 ft, the altitude of the APM's cruise payload/range charts: ISA T = 216.65 K (above 36,089 ft); a = 661.47 x sqrt(216.65 / 288.15) = 573.6 kt; TAS = 0.74 x 573.6 = 424.4 -> 425 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Tier 4. The same source gives high-speed cruise up to M0.81. At the Airliner preset's 35,000 ft the TAS would be 0.74 x 576.4 = 426.5 -> 425 kt, the same.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Takeoff weight midway between MLW 47,000 lb and MTOW 53,000 lb (APM Table 1, CRJ200 LR) = 50,000 lb. APM 00-03-01 p. 11 Figure 10 (FAR takeoff runway length, ISA, CF34-3B1, flaps 20, zero wind, zero runway gradient, zero engine bleed), read from the chart's vector paths: weight axis 34 klb at 581.6 pt, 45.6 pt per klb (50 klb at 217.05 pt); distance axis gridlines 6 thousand ft at 269.17 pt and 5 at 306.43 pt (a 200 ft minor gridline every 7.45 pt); the sea-level curve (rightmost) has a vertex at (284.05 pt, 217.03 pt), i.e. 50,000 lb and 6 - (284.05 - 269.17)/37.26 = 5.60 thousand ft = 5,600 ft (the 5,600 ft minor gridline is at 284.07 pt). Landing at MLW 47,000 lb, flaps 45, sea level, dry (Figure 21, p. 22, raster): about 4,800 ft (4.77 thousand ft). Longer = takeoff 5,600 ft (already a whole hundred).
min_runway_ft.note: Vector chart read against its gridlines; the sea-level curve's plotted vertex at 50,000 lb lies on the 5.6 thousand ft gridline, so 5,600 ft. Figure 21 is plotted for CF34-3A1 engines. Aircraft Commerce quotes a CRJ-200 LR take-off field length of 6,020 ft (conditions not given; the chart gives about 6.3 thousand ft at 53,000 lb) and landing 4,850 ft.

ceiling_ft.note: 'The aircraft is certified for a maximum altitude of 41,000 feet' (CL-600-2B19, Section 2 III). Aircraft Commerce agrees.

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude of the manufacturer's cruise payload/range charts (long range cruise and Mach 0.80 cruise at 37,000 ft), taken as its cruise altitude; the cruise speed above is not quoted at that altitude by the manufacturer (at the Airliner preset's 35,000 ft the same Mach gives the same 425 kt).

climb_kts.note: Airliner class preset: 90% of the 425 kt cruise speed = 382.5 -> 385 kt.

sources.page: Rows 'Cruise speed at 75% (6,000 ft)' 254 km/h TAS = 137 kts TAS; 'Take-off performance (MSL, ground roll / take-off obstacle)' 305 m / 450 m (1,476 ft); 'Landing performance (MSL, ground roll / landing distance)' 290 m / 620 m = 2,033 ft; 'Max. operating altitude 5,000 m 16,400 ft'; 'Max. demonstrated crosswind 37 km/h 20 kts'; 'Max. take off mass 1,200 kg'

pressurised.note: No accepted source states 'unpressurised' in words (TCDS A.022 is silent). The AFM describes no pressurisation system, says in 4A.3.19 that 'at high altitudes the provision of oxygen for the occupants is necessary' and requires supplemental oxygen above 14,000 ft for US-registered airplanes (2.11), and its alternate static source uses 'the static pressure in the cabin'. An inference from the manufacturer's manual, as for the DA62 entry: the checker may confirm or null it.

cruise_kts.note: Diamond's performance table (MTOM, ISA), DA40 XLT: 'Cruise speed at 75% (6,000 ft)' 254 km/h TAS = 137 kts TAS; names power and altitude. The same table's 'Max. cruise speed (MSL, MCP)' 142 kts is not used. The AFM's cruising-TAS diagram (5.3.9, p. 5-18), read at 6,000 ft density altitude (ISA) on the 75 % curve, gives about 137 kt, agreeing.

min_runway_ft.calculation: AFM 5.3.10 (p. 5-19), landing distance flaps LDG over a 50 ft (15 m) obstacle, ISA, MSL: approx. 638 m (2093 ft) at 1150 kg; 'a landing mass above 1150 kg up to 1200 kg will increase the landing distance ... up to 6 %': 638 x 1.06 = 676.3 m = 2219 ft at the 1200 kg maximum take-off mass; up to the next 100 ft = 2300 ft. Take-off over 50 ft at 1200 kg is shorter (AFM nomogram p. 5-13, whose example gives 300 m at 1000 kg, 2,000 ft, 10 kt headwind; Diamond's page 450 m).
min_runway_ft.note: Piston rule (max gross, 50 ft obstacle, the longer of take-off and landing). Diamond's spec page prints 620 m / 2,033 ft landing and 450 m take-off; the AFM, the manufacturer's certified document, gives the higher landing figure and is preferred, the marketing figure is not used. The AFM take-off nomogram was only roughly read: it is clearly below the landing figure.

ceiling_ft.note: EASA TCDS EASA.IM.A.022 Issue 24, DA 40, item 11: maximum operating altitude 5000 m (16 404 ft); AFM 2.11 'maximum demonstrated operating altitude is 16,400 ft (5,000 m)' (14,000 ft MSL for US-registered airplanes without oxygen).

max_xwind_kts.note: AFM 5.3.5 (p. 5-10): 'Max. demonstrated crosswind component: 20 kts'; Diamond's web page 'Max. demonstrated crosswind 37 km/h 20 kts'. Demonstrated, not a limit.

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude at which Diamond quotes the 75 % cruise speed.

climb_fpm.calculation: AFM 5.3.8 cruise-climb rate-of-climb diagram (p. 5-17; max power, 2400 RPM, flaps up, 76 KIAS at 1200 kg), 1200 kg (the diagram's bottom edge), ISA temperature at each altitude: sea level (15 C) about 785 fpm, 6,000 ft (3 C) about 490 fpm (reading of the printed diagram; 2,000 ft about 680, 4,000 ft about 585). Rate falling linearly: time to 6,000 ft = 6000/(785-490) x ln(785/490) = 9.6 min; 6000/9.6 = 627; the plain mean of the two rates is 638 -> 650 fpm
climb_fpm.note: No time to climb is published; this is worked from the AFM's rate-of-climb diagram at the cruise altitude of 6,000 ft, as for the Beaver entry. Diamond's headline rate of climb at MSL is 780 ft/min.

climb_kts.calculation: AFM 5.3.8 (p. 5-16): cruise-climb speed 76 KIAS at 1200 kg. TAS = 76 / sqrt(density ratio) in the ISA: 76 kt at sea level, 83 kt at 6,000 ft; averaged over the climb's time (the rate falls from 785 to 490 fpm, see climb rate) = 79.8 -> 80 kt
climb_kts.note: IAS taken as CAS (no position-error correction). The class preset would be 0.65 x 137 = 90 kt.

descent_fpm.note: Piston single class preset; no published descent rate or time found.

pressurised.calculation: The DC-10-30 is certified to a maximum operating altitude of 42,000 ft (A22WE p. 12 of 50) under FAR 25 Amendments 1-22 (p. 38 of 50), which requires a pressurised cabin (25.841) for flight above 25,000 ft.
pressurised.note: No accepted source found that says 'pressurised' of the DC-10 in so many words (the planning manual's text layer is unreadable); the finding rests on the certified ceiling and FAR 25, as for the MD-11 entry.

cruise_kts.calculation: Boeing's payload/range chart for the Series 30 is flown at 'Mach 0.82 cruise, 31,000/35,000 feet step altitude' (ACAP printed p. 47). Typical cruise taken as M0.82 at 35,000 ft, ISA: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81 / 288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.82 x 576.4 = 472.6 -> 475 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Boeing's planning manual gives no separate typical or economy cruise figure; M0.82 is its planning cruise Mach.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights: MTOW 572,000 lb and MLW 421,000 lb (ACAP printed p. 4 note 'For 572,000-pound MTOGW ... increase landing weight to 421,000 pounds'; chart limits on pp. 61 and 65); midpoint = (421,000 + 572,000) / 2 = 496,500 lb. Takeoff: ACAP printed p. 61, upper panel (standard day, zero wind, takeoff thrust, packs off), sea-level solid curve (CF6-50C), read by pixel position against the gridlines (380k lb at x=410.5, 500k lb at x=880.5; 8 thousand ft at y=780.5, 6 at y=856.5 on a 2.6x render): at 496,500 lb the curve's centre is on the 8,000 ft gridline, 7.99 thousand ft = about 7,990 ft (good to about +/-50 ft; the dashed CF6-50C1 curve is lower, about 7.6). Landing: printed p. 65, sea level at MLW 421,000 lb = about 6.15 thousand ft (flaps 50, dry; the left axis is thousand ft, the right axis thousand m). Longer = takeoff 7,990 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 8,000 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Chart readings are good to about 50 ft. The manual gives one landing flap setting (50). Takeoff governs.

ceiling_ft.note: FAA A22WE, Model DC-10-30 section: 'Maximum Operating Altitude: 42,000 feet' (p. 12 of 50).

cruise_alt_ft.calculation: The chart's cruise is a step cruise at 31,000 and 35,000 ft (ACAP printed p. 47); the typical cruise altitude is taken as the upper step, 35,000 ft, the altitude at which the cruise speed above is worked.

climb_fpm.note: Airliner class preset; Boeing's planning manual gives no time to climb.

climb_kts.note: Airliner class preset: 90% of the 475 kt cruise speed = 427.5 -> 430 kt.

descent_fpm.note: Airliner class preset; no published descent rate or time found.

pressurised.note: NTSB-AAR-79-7 quotes the DC-8 operating procedure 'Depressurize the airplane when below 10,000 feet', which states that the airplane is pressurised. The report is for a DC-8-61, not the DC-8-55: a variant of the same family and fuselage design, used under the published-variant fallback. cruise_kts.calculation: ACAP payload/range chart notes (p. 47): 'Initial cruise altitude is 30,000 ft ... Cruise at Mach 0.82 for ranges shorter than indicated by [circle]'. ISA at 30,000 ft: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 30000 = 228.71 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(228.71 / 288.15) = 589.3 kt; TAS = 0.82 x 589.3 = 483.2 -> 485 kt.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights (ACAP p. 4, DC-8-55 column; TCDS 4A25 Sec. XIV agrees): MTOW 325,000 lb, MLW 217,000 lb; midpoint = (217,000 + 325,000) / 2 = 271,000 lb. Landing at MLW 258,000 lb: ACAP p. 85 (PDF p. 89), dry (dashed) sea-level curve at the -63 maximum-landing-weight line (gridlines 260 klb y=806, 240 klb y=995.5; line centre y=827.5, 257.7 klb): curve at x=1142 between length gridlines 7 kft x=1064 and 6 kft x=1165.5: 7 - (1142 - 1064) / 101.5 = 6.23 kft = about 6,230 ft. cruise_kts.calculation: Boeing's DC-9 specification table gives 'Speed 550 mph' (statute miles per hour). 1 mph = 0.868976 kt: 550 x 0.868976 = 477.9 -> 478 kt (a published figure converted between units, kept in whole units).
cruise_kts.note: Maximum / headline cruise. Boeing's archived page prints one column headed 'DC-9' (rows: Model number 'DC-9/C-9', Wingspan 89 ft 4 in, Power plant 'Two 12,250-pound-thrust P&W JT8D', Weight 90,700 pounds, Ceiling 37,000 feet, Speed 550 mph, Accommodation 70 to 172 passengers); no series is named and it is a family headline (its weight is the -10's, its ceiling the DC-9-80's, its seating spans the family). No Mach number or altitude is given. FAA TCDS A6WE gives the same MMO, M0.84, for the DC-9-11 to -15 (Section I) and the -31/-32 (Sections II, IV), so the family figure is used for both series as the maximum (headline) cruise. It is not a rule-10 case with the MD-80 (different wing, and the MD-80 Mach 0.76 is its own figure). 550 mph = 478 kt = about M0.81 at 30,000 ft, below MMO M0.84. No typical Mach found in the ACAP's payload-range pages (the only cruise pages; they name an altitude and no Mach) or any accepted source.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights (ACAP p. 4, column DC-9-15; TCDS Section I agrees): MTOW 90,700 lb, MLW 81,700 lb; midpoint = (81,700 + 90,700) / 2 = 86,200 lb. Takeoff: ACAP p. 46 (JT8D-1, lower chart 'STD DAY', zero wind and gradient, maximum takeoff power), sea-level curve at 86,200 lb. Read on a 4x render (upright): gridlines 85 klb x=1467 and 90 klb x=1675 put 86,200 lb at x=1517; local gridlines 6 kft y=560.0 and 0 kft y=901.5 (56.9 px/kft); the sea-level curve (the lowest of the five altitude curves) centre y=573.5; 6 - (573.5 - 560.0) / 56.9 = 5.76 kft (5.74 kft with whole-width gridlines) = about 5,750 ft. Landing at MLW 81,700 lb, ACAP p. 51 (flaps full down, standard day, dry runway = dashed sea-level line at the max-landing-weight line): about 5,050 ft. Longer = takeoff about 5,750 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 5,800 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Takeoff governs by about 700 ft. The readings are of a scanned chart (about +/-0.1 kft); both gridline treatments give 5,740-5,760 ft, which rounds up to 5,800 ft.

pressurised.note: NZ CAA's type acceptance report (a government publication validating Transport Canada type certificate A-142) calls the DHC-8 a 'high wing pressurised twin turboprop'. EASA TCDS IM.A.191 gives no cabin pressure line, but lists the pressurised-cabin-loads requirement FAR 25.365(e) in the Series 200 certification basis (p. 14). The DHC-8-400 section of NZ's report (p. 5) also says 'The pressurized cabin is equipped to operate up to an altitude of 25,000 feet'.

cruise_kts.note: 'Maximum Cruise Speed' 360 kt (DHC spec sheet, enroute figures for the EHGW variant, 82 passengers); 'High cruise speed 360 kts' (Media Guide p. 4.01). Neither names power or altitude, so this is the manufacturer's headline cruise speed, noted as such (meanings table, last alternative). Aircraft Commerce issue 63 p. 7 tabulates 360 kt for the Q402 EHGW too (not cited).

min_runway_ft.note: Media Guide p. 4.01: FAR takeoff field length (SL, ISA) at MTOW 4,694 ft (1,431 m); FAR landing field length (SL) at MLW 4,232 ft (1,290 m). Takeoff is the longer. MTOW 65,200 lb / MLW 62,000 lb are the heaviest (EHGW) weights, matching the variant. DHC's current spec sheet gives lower figures (takeoff 4,188 ft at MTOW, landing 4,160 ft at MLW) but states they are for the Basic Gross Weight variant, so they do not describe this variant; noted for the checker. Rule 5 (heaviest weights): the 2008 Media Guide figure is for MTOW 65,200 lb (EHGW); the 2026 sheet's airfield figures are for the Basic Gross Weight variant, so the Media Guide governs. Both are the manufacturer's.

ceiling_ft.note: EASA TCDS Section 5 (Series 400), item 11, p. 31; DHC spec sheet 'Maximum Cruise Altitude 25,000 ft' and Media Guide p. 4.01 agree. Maximum operating altitude 7,620 m (25,000 ft), pressure altitude; the same for every DHC-8 series.

max_xwind_kts.note: Bombardier's published guidance, Media Guide p. 1.04: 'approval to operate in crosswinds up to 32 knots (59.3 km/h) and tailwinds up to 20 knots'. Not stated as the AFM's demonstrated value, so it is the manufacturer's published crosswind guidance. Whole-unit published guidance; dry/wet not stated.

cruise_alt_ft.note: Turboprop preset 24,000 ft (under the 25,000 ft ceiling; pressurised).

climb_kts.note: Turboprop preset fraction 0.6 x 360 kt cruise = 216 kt, rounded to 5 kt.

sources.page: Section IV para 4.10.1 'Performance at maximum gross weight, standard conditions', pp. 40-41 (PDF pp. 58-59); Section II para 2.14.2 p. 26 (PDF p. 40); Section II para 2.10 p. 24 (PDF p. 38); Appendix Cruise Power Chart (PDF p. 89)

cruise_kts.calculation: Flight manual p. 40, landplane 5,100 lb, standard conditions: 'True Cruising Speed (300 BHP)' at 5,000 ft = 143 mph (230 km/h); at sea level 136 mph. 143 mph x 0.868976 kt/mph = 124.3 -> 124 kt (unit conversion only).
cruise_kts.note: 300 BHP is the manual's highest tabulated cruise power (about 67% of the engine's 450 hp; the manual gives no 75% figure; the 240 BHP economic cruise gives 130 mph at 5,000 ft). 5,000 ft is the higher of the two altitudes tabulated. The manual's 'Max. True Level Speed' (163 mph at 5,000 ft) is not a cruise figure.

min_runway_ft.note: Flight manual p. 40, landplane, 5,100 lb, standard conditions, flaps 'Take-off'/'Landing', still air, ICAO technique: take-off distance to clear a 50 ft obstacle 1,250 ft (381 m); landing distance over a 50 ft obstacle 1,250 ft (381 m). Equal.

ceiling_ft.note: Flight manual p. 40, 'Service Ceiling' 18,000 ft (5,490 m), landplane. No maximum operating altitude is certified in the manual.

max_xwind_kts.calculation: Flight manual para 2.14.2 (p. 26): 'The lateral component of wind velocity at and below which it is safe to take off and land is not more than 10 mph at 90 deg for landplane, skiplane and seaplane.' 10 mph x 0.868976 = 8.69 -> 9 kt (unit conversion only).
max_xwind_kts.note: The manufacturer's guidance for safe take-off and landing, not described as 'demonstrated'.

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude at which the flight manual's cruising speed is quoted (5,000 ft, also the altitude of its range and endurance figures).

climb_fpm.calculation: Flight manual p. 41, landplane 5,100 lb, rate of climb at max. continuous power: sea level 840 fpm, 5,000 ft 795 fpm. Rate falling linearly with height (slope -45 fpm per 5,000 ft = -0.009 per min), time to 5,000 ft = (1/0.009) x ln(840/795) = 6.12 min; 5,000 / 6.12 = 817 fpm (the plain mean of the two rates, 817.5, agrees) -> 800 fpm (nearest 50).
climb_fpm.note: No time to climb is published; this average is worked from the two tabulated rates (max. continuous power, 2,200 rpm, 33.5 in.Hg, the power the manual prescribes for best rate of climb, para 2.10).

climb_kts.calculation: Flight manual para 2.10 (p. 24): speed for best rate of climb 95 mph IAS (also shown as 82 knots in Fig. 3-1). 95 mph = 82.6 kt IAS. TAS at the climb's mid-height 2,500 ft, ISA: density ratio 0.9289, sqrt = 0.9638; 82.6 / 0.9638 = 85.7 -> 85 kt (nearest 5 kt; IAS taken as CAS, no position-error correction).
climb_kts.note: Indicated best-rate speed 95 mph (82.6 kt) from para 2.10 (p. 24), converted to true airspeed at the climb's mid-height (the mean of TAS at sea level 82.6 and at 5,000 ft 88.9 gives the same 85.7); IAS taken as CAS.

descent_fpm.note: Piston single class preset. The manual gives only an approximate 1,000 ft/min on the 80 mph final approach (para 2.13) and 890 fpm engine-out glide, not a normal descent rate.

This was the maximum encountered during crosswind landing trials, and is not considered limiting." The 20 kt is kept as the demonstrated value (landing; the AFM gives no demonstrated figure for take-off or other flap settings, TSB A13A0033 footnote 2). sources.publisher: Cessna Aircraft Company (scan hosted by aeroelectric.com)
sources.page: Printed p. ii 'Performance and Specifications' (1 June 1988 revision; PDF p. 6): weights, speed at 8,300 lb max cruise power at 15,000 ft 246 KTAS, rate of climb 1851 fpm, service ceiling all engines above 30,000 ft, takeoff total distance over 50-ft obstacle 2635 ft at 9360 lb, landing over 50-ft obstacle 2485 ft; p. 2-18 (Maximum Operating Altitude is 30,000 feet); p. 4-3 item (10) and p. 5-21 note (demonstrated crosswind 20 knots, not a limitation); p. 5-49 Figure 5-23 time, fuel and distance to climb, cruise climb, climb speeds 140/125/110 KIAS (PDF p. 217); p. 5-102 Figure 5-34 time, fuel and distance to descend at 750 fpm (PDF p. 270)

pressurised.calculation: Neither the manufacturer's manual nor the EASA data sheet describes a cabin pressurisation system or a cabin pressure differential limit (the PA-46 data sheet, for contrast, lists one); the manual's limitations cap flight at 30,000 ft and its emergency and normal procedures carry only an optional 'oxygen system (if installed)' and ram-air cabin controls.
pressurised.note: No accepted source states 'unpressurised' in words; kept on the omission in both documents (as for the SR22 entries). Secondary sites say non-pressurised.

cruise_kts.note: Cessna's headline speed at maximum cruise power at 15,000 ft, 8,300 lb (mid-cruise weight), standard day: 246 KTAS (p. ii); Figure 5-32 shows the same 246 KTAS on its maximum cruise power curve at about 16,500 ft.

min_runway_ft.note: Takeoff total distance over a 50-ft obstacle at 9,360 lb, wing flaps T.O., standard day, level dry hard surface, no wind (ground roll 2,121 ft); landing over 50 ft at 9,360 lb 2,485 ft (ground roll 1,327 ft). Takeoff is longer. The accelerate-stop field length (4,227 ft) and landing field length (4,143 ft, 1/.6 factor) are regulatory lengths, not used.

ceiling_ft.note: Certified maximum operating altitude: POH p. 2-18 and TCDS item 11, 30,000 ft. The manual's service ceiling, all engines, is 'above 30,000 feet'.

max_xwind_kts.note: Maximum demonstrated crosswind velocity 20 knots (p. 4-3 item 10; p. 5-21 note: 'not a limitation').

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude at which Cessna quotes the 246 KTAS maximum cruise speed (p. ii).

climb_fpm.calculation: Figure 5-23 (p. 5-49, cruise climb, power levers maximum cruise, initial weight 9,360 lb): entering at the ISA line at 15,000 ft (-15 C, midway between the 14 and 16 thousand-foot curves where they meet the ISA line), across to the 9,360 lb curve, down to the time scale: about 8.7 min (scale 0 at the sea-level reading, which adds nothing at a sea-level airport). 15000 ft / 8.7 min = 1724 -> 1700 fpm.
climb_fpm.note: Read from the scanned chart, good to about +/-0.4 min (1,650-1,800 fpm). Chart conditions: cruise climb at 140 KIAS to 12,000 ft, 125 KIAS above; the manual's sea-level all-engine rate is 1851 fpm.

climb_kts.calculation: Same Figure 5-23 reading, distance scale below the time scale at the same point: about 22 nm to climb to 15,000 ft in about 8.7 min. 22.3 nm / 8.7 min x 60 = 154 -> 155 kt average true airspeed over the climb's time (published distance / time).
climb_kts.note: Distance read from the chart to about +/-1 nm; time and distance move together along the curve, so the ratio holds (a 9.3 min / 23.9 nm reading gives the same 154 kt). Replaces an average over altitude of the IAS schedule.

descent_fpm.note: Figure 5-34 (p. 5-102) is drawn for a 750 FPM rate of descent, power as required, 180 KIAS, gear and flaps up, propeller 1900 RPM (10,000 ft descent takes 13.3 min in the manual's example).

sources.page: Cover panel 'Dimensions and Characteristics' (Maximum Gross Takeoff Weight 496,000 lb; Maximum Landing Weight 368,000 lb); PDF p. 2 'Performance' (cruise 'at a cruise speed of Mach 0.83'; chart 'Dash 500 Airport Performance', sea level, 15 C day, FAR takeoff and landing field length against aircraft weight)

pressurised.calculation: The data sheet certifies Model L-1011-385-3 to a maximum operating altitude of 43,000 ft (A23WE p. 18 of 23), under a certification basis of FAR Part 25 of 1 February 1965 (p. 19 of 23), whose pressurised-cabin rules (25.841) a transport flying that high must meet; an unpressurised cabin is not possible at that ceiling.
pressurised.note: The data sheet does not use the word 'pressurised'; no complete accepted document found that does (Lockheed's Technical Profile scan lacks printed pp. 4-5 and is not cited). Derived from the certified ceiling.

cruise_kts.calculation: Lockheed's brochure gives the cruise as Mach 0.83 ('Mach 0.83 cruise, ISA' on the payload-range chart; 'at a cruise speed of Mach 0.83'). Typical cruise altitude taken as the Airliner preset's 35,000 ft (the brochure names none), ISA: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81 / 288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.83 x 576.4 = 478.4 -> 480 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Lockheed names no typical or economy cruise Mach other than this one; the data sheet's Mmo is M0.90. The 35,000 ft is the preset, not a published altitude; above 36,089 ft the same Mach gives a lower TAS only by the temperature floor (M0.83 = 477 kt at FL390).

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights from Lockheed's brochure: MTOW 496,000 lb, MLW 368,000 lb; midpoint = (368,000 + 496,000) / 2 = 432,000 lb. Chart 'Dash 500 Airport Performance' (sea level, 15 C day), read by pixel position against the gridlines (x: 240 to 520 thousand lb across the plot; y: 6,000 and 8,000 ft gridlines 59 px per 1,000 ft): FAR takeoff field length at 432,000 lb = 6,675 ft; FAR landing field length at MLW 368,000 lb = about 6,360 ft. Longer = takeoff 6,675 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,700 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: The chart names no flap setting and its takeoff curve ends at about 498,000 lb (the brochure's MTOW); the FAA data sheet (A23WE p. 17 of 23) certifies 504,000 and 510,000 lb takeoff weights too, for which Lockheed's brochure gives no chart, and its landing curve stops at about 380,000 lb. Chart readings are good to about 50 ft. Standard day is 15 C (ISA).

ceiling_ft.note: Certified maximum operating altitude: 'Maximum Operating Altitude 43,000 ft. Models L-1011-385-1-15 and -3' (A23WE p. 18 of 23).

pressurised.calculation: The type is certified to a maximum operating altitude of 43,200 ft (FAA A22WE p. 27 of 50; EASA IM.A.210 p. 16 of 21). Part 25, the certification basis (A22WE p. 38 of 50), requires a pressurised cabin (25.841) for flight above 25,000 ft: a pressurised cabin. The NTSB's Newark report (p. 14) treats a ferry flight of an MD-11 as an exception when 'unpressurized'.
pressurised.note: No accepted source found that says in so many words that the MD-11 is pressurised (neither data sheet; the planning manual's text layer is unreadable; the FAA FSB report only lists 'Pressurization' as a systems-difference training item); the finding rests on the certified ceiling, Part 25 and the NTSB's wording.

cruise_kts.calculation: Boeing's payload-range chart is flown as 'STEP CRUISE AT 31-35-39,000 FT AT MACH 0.82' (ACAP p. 3-2). Typical cruise taken as M0.82 at the middle step, 35,000 ft, ISA: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81 / 288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.82 x 576.4 = 472.6 -> 475 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Boeing's airport-planning manual gives no separate typical or economy cruise figure; M0.82 is the manufacturer's planning cruise Mach for the type (the data sheet's Mmo is M0.87). Boeing's own MD-11 product page could not be opened (see research_notes). Same method as the A340 entries.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights: MTOW 630,500 lb and MLW 458,000 lb (FAA A22WE p. 26 of 50: landing 458,000 lb at every takeoff weight; ACAP p. 2-2 Combi column 630,500 / 458,000 lb); midpoint = (458,000 + 630,500) / 2 = 544,250 lb. Takeoff: ACAP p. 3-10 (CF6-80C2D1F, standard day, zero wind, zero slope), sea-level curve at 544,250 lb read by pixel position against the gridlines: 7.93 thousand ft = 7,930 ft. Landing at MLW 458,000 lb, dry, sea level: p. 3-17 (flaps 50) about 7,220 ft, p. 3-16 (flaps 35) about 7,880 ft. Longer = takeoff 7,930 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 8,000 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: The manual names no normal landing flap setting, so the shortest (flaps 50) applies; takeoff governs with either. Chart readings are good to about 30 ft. The passenger 'ER' column (MLW 430,000 lb) is lighter; rule 5 takes the heaviest design weights, which the FAA data sheet confirms. With 430,000 lb the midpoint (530,250 lb) would read 7,570 ft -> 7,600 ft. The takeoff chart is one chart for the MD-11 with GE engines.

ceiling_ft.note: Certified maximum operating altitude: FAA A22WE 'Maximum Operating Altitude: 43,200 feet' (p. 27 of 50) and EASA IM.A.210 p. 16 of 21, 12,800 m (43,200 ft) pressure altitude. The two agree.

cruise_alt_ft.calculation: The chart's cruise is a step cruise at 31,000, 35,000 and 39,000 ft (ACAP p. 3-2); the typical cruise altitude is taken as the middle step, 35,000 ft.

climb_kts.note: Airliner class preset: 90% of the 475 kt cruise speed = 427.5 -> 430 kt.

descent_fpm.note: Airliner class preset; no published descent rate or time found.

min_runway_ft.calculation: Weights (ACAP p. 2-2, column MD-82, -88): MTOW 149,500 lb, MLW 130,000 lb; midpoint = (130,000 + 149,500) / 2 = 139,750 lb. Takeoff: ACAP p. 3-12 (JT8D-217A, 'MD-82 and -88', lower chart 'STD DAY', zero wind and gradient, normal takeoff thrust), sea-level curve at 139,750 lb. Read on a 300 dpi render rotated upright: gridlines 130 klb x=342.5 and 140 klb x=533.1 (19.06 px/klb) put 139,750 lb at x=528.3; 6 kft line y=717.2 and 8 kft line y=524.6 at that x (tilt of the scan allowed for; 96.3 px/kft); sea-level curve centre (centroid fit over x=440-640) y=706.1; 6 + (717.2 - 706.1) / 96.3 = 6.115 kft = 6,115 ft. Landing at MLW 130,000 lb, ACAP p. 3-16 (flaps 40, dry, sea level, standard day): about 4,700 ft. Longer = takeoff 6,115 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,200 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Takeoff governs by about 1,400 ft. The takeoff reading lies close to the 6,100 ft rounding line: the first reader had 6,094 ft (6,100), the check measured 6,115 ft (6,200); chart readings are good to about +/-20 ft, so the true figure may sit on either side of 6,100, and the up-to-the-next-100 rule gives 6,200 for the reading taken. ACAP p. 3-11 also has a JT8D-217 chart; the -217A chart (p. 3-12, shared with the -88) is used. Flaps 40 is the shorter of the two landing charts (flaps 28 on p. 3-15); either landing figure is far below the takeoff.

Taken at the typical cruise altitude 35,000 ft (top step of the ACAP's long-range cruise, p. 3-2), ISA: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.81 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.81 / 288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.76 x 576.4 = 438.1 -> 440 kt.

Takeoff: ACAP p. 3-4 Fig. 3.3.1 (standard day, V2500-D5, normal takeoff thrust and ART, zero wind and gradient), sea-level curve, read from the PDF's vector path against the gridlines (110 klb and 4 kft/6 kft lines calibrated): plotted points (150.0 klb, 6.114 kft), (153.2 klb, 6.501 kft), (156.1 klb, 6.951 kft); straight line at 155.0 klb: 6.501 + (155.0 - 153.2)/(156.1 - 153.2) x (6.951 - 6.501) = 6.78-6.80 kft (checker re-read: 6.795 kft). Landing at MLW 142,000 lb, ACAP p. 3-6 Fig. 3.4.1 (flap 28, dry, sea level, standard day): about 5,500 ft (visual read; flap 40 on the next page is shorter). Longer = takeoff about 6,790 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 6,800 ft.

Fig. 3.3.1 is titled MD-90-30/-30ER and its plotted weights end at 156,000 lb (dashed line labelled 'Maximum design takeoff weight = 156,000 lb', the -30's MTOW), so the ER's own MTOW (168,000 lb) is off the chart; the ER midpoint 155,000 lb is an interpolation inside the plotted range, not an extrapolation. At the base -30's weights (MTOW 156,000, MLW 142,000; midpoint 149,000 lb) the same curve gives about 6.03 kft -> 6,100 ft. The ACAP's note: not to be used for flight planning.

cruise_kts.calculation: 'The 250 Comanche has a maximum recommended cruising speed of 181 M.P.H. at 75% power at 7000 feet' (Owner's Handbook p. 25; also p. 1, optimum cruising speed, 75% power, 181 mph): 181 mph / 1.15078 = 157.3 kt -> 157 kt (a published figure converted to knots, kept in whole units)
cruise_kts.note: TAS (the handbook's speeds are true airspeeds, p. 25). At 75% power at sea level the handbook gives 171 mph (p. 1).

min_runway_ft.note: Take-off total distance over 50 ft barrier at 2,900 lb (max gross), sea level, 60°F (the table's row nearest the 59°F standard day), zero wind, 15° Max-Lift flaps (the handbook's only PA-24-250 take-off table; ground run 1,180 ft). Landing over 50 ft barrier at 2,900 lb, sea level, 60°F, zero wind: 1,420 ft (p. 28).

ceiling_ft.note: Manufacturer's service ceiling (1A15 certifies no maximum operating altitude). Absolute ceiling 22,000 ft.

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude at which the handbook quotes the 181 mph cruise (p. 25).

climb_fpm.note: The handbook gives rates of climb (1,350 fpm at sea level, p. 1; rate-of-climb chart p. 42) but no time to climb.

climb_kts.calculation: Climb schedule (p. 24): best rate of climb 105 mph IAS at sea level, decreasing about 1 mph per 1,000 ft, so 98 mph IAS at 7,000 ft. IAS taken as CAS (no position-error data); TAS = CAS / sqrt(sigma), ISA sigma(7,000 ft) = 0.8106. Sea level: 105 mph = 91.2 kt TAS; 7,000 ft: 98 mph = 85.2 kt CAS = 94.6 kt TAS. Average over the climb ≈ (91.2 + 94.6) / 2 = 92.9 kt (a time-weighted average using the p. 42 rate-of-climb line gives 93.0 kt) → 95 kt
climb_kts.note: The handbook also says a good climb is obtained at 100-110 mph at lower altitudes with more forward speed.

sources.page: PDF page 7 of 22 (A.III item 2 Description: 'Twin engine reciprocating, all-metal, four-place, unpressurized, low wing aeroplane'; item 5 Engines: O-360-E1A6D / LO-360-E1A6D for S/Ns 44-7995001 through 44-8195026); PDF page 9 (item 10 Maximum Operating Altitude: 'no limitation specified', PA-44-180)

sources.title: Piper 1979 PA-44-180 Seminole, Specifications (service ceiling 17,100 ft; cruise speed 75% power 166 kts)
sources.page: Specifications table of the 'Piper 1979 PA-44-180 Seminole' page (Lyc. O-360-A-E1AD, 180 hp; service ceiling 17,100 ft; cruise speed 166 kts at 75% power); a web page of the magazine's model-aircraft guide, no print issue given

pressurised.note: EASA TCDS IM.A.232 describes the PA-44-180 as 'unpressurized'.

cruise_kts.calculation: POH Figure 5-31 Speed Power (p. 5-26, mid-cruise weight 3,483 lb, cowl flaps closed, 2-blade propellers) at standard temperature. The 75% performance-cruise line ends at the 2700 rpm full-throttle limit, at the 8,000 ft pressure-altitude level where the STD TEMP line crosses it (on the scan the top of the 75% line is at y = 1013 px and 8,000 ft at standard temperature falls at y = 1015 px, fitted from the chart's own altitude lines), so 75% power is fastest there. True-airspeed axis (gridlines at 120, 140, 160, 180 kt, 7.475 px/kt): the top of the 75% line is at 160 + (1611 - 1560)/7.475 = 166.8 kt -> 165 kt.
cruise_kts.note: Reading good to about +/-1 kt. Plane & Pilot's table gives 166 kt at 75% power for the 1979 O-360 aeroplane, the same. Piper's 2023 spec sheet 'Max Cruise Speed 162 ktas' names neither power nor altitude and is for the IO-360-B1G6 aeroplane, so it is not used.

min_runway_ft.calculation: POH Figure 5-11 Normal Procedure Takeoff Distance Over 50 Ft Barrier (p. 5-16; 2700 rpm full throttle, flaps 0, paved level dry runway): sea level at 15 C (chart y = 1006 px), 3,800 lb (the reference line), zero wind, read on the distance axis (1,000 ft at y = 1185 px, 14.85 px per 100 ft): 1000 + (1185 - 1006)/0.1485 = 2205 ft -> 2,200 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Chart reading good to about +/-20 ft, so 2,200 ft. Landing over 50 ft (Figure 5-45, short field effort, p. 5-33) reads about 1,400 ft at 3,800 lb, so the takeoff is the longer. Piper's 2023 spec sheet for the IO-360-B1G6 Seminole gives 2,200 ft takeoff and 1,490 ft landing over a 50 ft obstacle, the same takeoff (not used: another engine variant).

ceiling_ft.note: Fourth-tier source: Plane & Pilot's table for the 1979 O-360 PA-44-180, 'Service ceiling 17,100 ft'. The EASA TCDS gives 'no limitation specified' for the PA-44-180 (item 10, PDF p. 9; the 20,000 ft limit in the same sheet is the PA-44-180T's) and the POH states no service ceiling, so no authority or Piper figure exists in the first three tiers. Enthusiast sites list 15,000 ft (a twin-engine 100 fpm ceiling); not cited.

max_xwind_kts.note: 'DEMONSTRATED CROSSWIND COMPONENT 17 KTS' on the required instrument-panel placard (POH section 2.27, p. 2-7), 'Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Velocity' (section 4, p. 4-2) and 'maximum demonstrated crosswind component for landing is 17 KTS' (p. 4-25).

cruise_alt_ft.calculation: Altitude at which the POH's 75% power line is fastest (Figure 5-31, standard temperature): the top of the 75% line is at the 8,000 ft level (see cruise speed); 8,000 ft.
cruise_alt_ft.note: Below the 12,000 ft cap for an unpressurised type and the 17,100 ft ceiling; equal to the Piston twin preset's altitude.

climb_fpm.calculation: POH Figure 5-27 (p. 5-24; 88 KIAS, both engines, 2700 rpm full throttle, flaps 0, gear up, cowl flaps open, no wind): at the standard-temperature point of 8,000 ft (chart y = 821 px) the TIME line reads 7.89 min on the 15.05 px/unit axis (line at x = 1480 px, axis zero at 1361 px); sea level at standard temperature (y = 1412 px) reads 0.2 min. 7.89 - 0.2 = 7.7 min; 8000 / 7.7 = 1039 -> 1050 fpm.
climb_fpm.note: Chart reading, about +/-0.3 min (about +/-40 fpm). The POH's sea-level rate of climb at 3,800 lb (Fig 5-23) reads 1,341 fpm, and integrating Fig 5-23's rates over 0-8,000 ft gives about 8.2 min (about 1,000 fpm), within the reading error. The chart's printed example (4.5 min at 5,500 ft) is below what its drawn lines give; the lines are used.

climb_kts.calculation: Same Figure 5-27 reading: the DISTANCE line reads 12.78 NM at 8,000 ft (x = 1553 px) less 0.2 NM at sea level = 12.6 NM in 7.7 min: 12.6 / 7.7 x 60 = 98.2 -> 100 kt (published distance / time).
climb_kts.note: Chart reading, about +/-0.4 NM and +/-0.3 min (95-100 kt). True airspeed at 88 KIAS is about 88 kt at sea level and 98 kt at 8,000 ft, so the time average should be nearer 94 kt; 98.2 is what the chart's lines give and is kept, rounding to 100.

descent_fpm.note: POH Figure 5-41 (p. 5-31) is drawn for 'Both engines 2400 RPM & throttle as required to maintain 165 KIAS and 500 FPM descent'. The chart's time line agrees: about 15.4 min from 8,000 ft at standard temperature (8000 / 15.4 = 520 fpm).

Neither says 'unpressurised' in words; this rests on their silence about a system they would have to describe.

cruise_kts.note: Handbook headline 'Cruise, 75% Power at 7500 Ft ... 156 KNOTS' (Performance - Specifications p. ii); it names power and altitude. Maximum at sea level 160 kt. The cruise charts (Fig 5-7) show about 151-154 KTAS at 75% near 8,000 ft; the headline is used as the meanings table asks.

min_runway_ft.note: Total distance over a 50 ft obstacle: takeoff 1,570 ft (flaps 20, 3,100 lb, sea level, 15 C, paved dry level runway, zero wind; Figure 5-4 gives 1,515 ft at 10 C and 1,625 ft at 20 C, which average 1,570); landing over 50 ft 1,320 ft. The longer is the takeoff.

ceiling_ft.note: Service ceiling 14,300 ft; the handbook's footnote: 18,000 ft if an optional EGT indicator is used to set the mixture. The TCDS certifies no maximum operating altitude.

max_xwind_kts.note: 'Maximum Demonstrated Crosswind Velocity: Takeoff or Landing 18 knots' (Section 4 p. 4-3); not a limitation.

cruise_alt_ft.note: The altitude at which the handbook quotes its 156 kt, 75% power cruise. Below the 14,300 ft ceiling and the 12,000 ft unpressurised cap.

climb_fpm.calculation: Figure 5-6 sheet 2 (p. 5-16), normal climb 95 KIAS, 3,100 lb, flaps up, gear up, 2400 rpm, 23 in Hg or full throttle, standard temperature, from sea level: 6000 ft = 9 min, 15 NM; 8000 ft = 12 min, 21 NM. 7,500 ft is not tabulated; linear between: 10.5 min, 18 NM. 7500 / 10.5 = 714 -> 700 fpm.
climb_fpm.note: The handbook's normal enroute climb (Section 4 p. 4-3: 90-100 KIAS) is the schedule used, as for the C182 entry; the maximum-rate-of-climb sheet (Figure 5-6 sheet 1, p. 5-15) would give 800 fpm (9.25 min). Time is from sea level, not brake release; 2.0 gal for start, taxi and takeoff are separate.

climb_kts.calculation: Figure 5-6 sheet 2: distance to climb to 7,500 ft (linear between 6,000 ft = 15 NM and 8,000 ft = 21 NM) = 18 NM in 10.5 min. 18 / (10.5/60) = 102.9 kt -> 105 kt.
climb_kts.note: Zero-wind distance taken as air distance. Normal climb schedule 95 KIAS; the maximum-rate sheet would give 90 kt.

descent_fpm.note: No published descent rate or time to descend in the handbook; Piston single class preset.

climb_fpm.note: Airliner class preset; no published time to climb. (Rohr's claim of a shorter time to climb, found only on listing sites, has no accepted source.)

pressurised.note: Stated in words by the AAIB: the BAe 146's pressurisation system has a controller that holds the selected cabin altitude by modulating two cabin air discharge valves (AAIB Bulletin 1/2000; the aircraft in it is a Series 300, the system is the BAe 146's). The FAA's AD 2004-18-07, which names the whole BAe 146 / Avro 146-RJ family, concerns those pressurization discharge valves and cabin pressure controllers.

cruise_kts.calculation: Normal (minimum cost) cruise Mach 0.70 (PWK0043 p. 3 Operating Speeds table: Cruise 'Vmo / M0.70 / MCT'). At 35,000 ft (Airliner preset altitude, equal to the 35,000 ft ceiling), ISA: T = 288.15 - 0.0019812 x 35000 = 218.8 K; a = 661.47 x sqrt(218.8/288.15) = 576.4 kt; TAS = 0.70 x 576.4 = 403.5 -> 405 kt.
cruise_kts.note: The manufacturer states no altitude for the cruise Mach, so the preset altitude is used (the type's own ceiling is 35,000 ft).

min_runway_ft.calculation: PWK0043 p. 2 Airfield Performance, Take-off Field Length chart 'ISA, sea level' (JAR reserves, level paved runway, maximum passenger payload, 6 abreast, optional 33 deg flap): the RJ100 curve is plotted against still-air range, not weight, so no midpoint-weight reading exists; its end (1,000 nm, near the maximum-payload range limit, i.e. about MTOW) reads about 1550 m = 1550 x 3.28084 = 5085 ft. Landing field length, dry, sea level, normal approach (same page): 1,211 m (3,973 ft) at the stated payload, shorter. Longer = takeoff 5085 ft -> up to the next 100 ft = 5100 ft.
min_runway_ft.note: Chart read from the rendered figure against its gridlines (about +/-10 m). Takeoff taken at the chart's end as the MTOW figure because the chart has no weight axis. The landing figure is at a typical payload, not MLW, but is far shorter.
